lessons.title: Introduction to Painting and Decorating in Africa
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 1 of your Painting and Decorating training. This lesson sets the foundation for a successful career or business in the painting and decorating trade across Africa. We will explore what the trade involves, why it matters, and how you can position yourself for profit. Painting and decorating is not just about slapping paint on a wall. It is a skilled trade that combines surface preparation, product knowledge, colour theory, and business acumen. In many African countries, the construction and real estate sectors are booming. New homes, offices, hotels, and shopping centres are being built every day. Each of these structures needs painting and decorating. This creates a steady demand for skilled professionals. However, the market is also competitive. To stand out, you must offer quality work, reliable service, and fair pricing. Let us start by defining the scope of the trade. Painting includes interior and exterior walls, ceilings, floors, and metal surfaces. Decorating includes wallpapering, stencilling, faux finishes, and other decorative techniques. In Africa, we also have unique considerations such as intense sunlight, high humidity in coastal areas, dust in arid regions, and the prevalence of cement, mud, and stone surfaces. You must learn to work with these conditions. For example, in coastal cities like Mombasa or Lagos, salt air can corrode metal and cause paint to peel. You need to use corrosion-resistant primers and exterior paints with UV inhibitors. In dusty areas like the Sahel, surfaces must be cleaned thoroughly before painting to ensure adhesion. In rural areas, you may encounter mud walls that require special sealers before painting. Understanding your local environment is key to delivering lasting results. Now, let us talk about the business side. Many painters in Africa work as informal labourers, earning low daily wages. But you can elevate yourself by becoming a professional contractor. This means registering your business, obtaining a tax identification number, and possibly getting a trade certification. It also means marketing your services, managing clients, and pricing your work correctly. A professional painter in Africa can earn between 20,000 and 100,000 naira per project, depending on the size and location. In East Africa, a similar range in Kenyan shillings or Tanzanian shillings applies. The key is to move from daily labour to project-based contracts. To do this, you need a portfolio of your work. Take before-and-after photos of every job. Ask satisfied clients for testimonials. Create a simple business card or flyer. Use social media platforms like WhatsApp, Facebook, and Instagram to showcase your work. Many African clients find service providers through these channels. Also, consider partnering with real estate agents, interior designers, and construction companies. They can refer clients to you. Another important aspect is safety. Painting involves chemicals, dust, and sometimes working at heights. You must wear protective gear such as gloves, masks, and safety goggles. When working on scaffolding, ensure it is stable. In Africa, many accidents happen because of poor safety practices. Protect yourself and your workers. Finally, think about continuous learning. The painting industry is always evolving. New products, tools, and techniques emerge regularly. Attend workshops, join trade associations, and read industry magazines. The more you know, the more value you can offer. In this module, we will cover five lessons. Lesson 1 is this introduction. Lesson 2 will cover tools and materials. Lesson 3 will focus on surface preparation. Lesson 4 will teach you painting techniques. Lesson 5 will guide you on starting and running your painting business. By the end of this module, you will have a solid foundation to begin your journey as a professional painter and decorator in Africa. Remember, this trade can be lucrative if you approach it with skill, professionalism, and a business mindset. Let us get started.

lessons.title: Essential Tools and Materials for African Painters
lessons.body: In this lesson, we will explore the essential tools and materials you need as a painter and decorator in Africa. Having the right equipment is crucial for efficiency, quality, and safety. We will also discuss how to source these items locally and how to maintain them. First, let us talk about tools. You will need a variety of brushes. For large wall areas, use a wide brush, about 100mm to 150mm. For cutting in around edges, use a 50mm angled brush. For detailed work, use a 25mm sash brush. In Africa, you can find brushes at local hardware stores or markets. Look for brushes with synthetic bristles, as they work well with both water-based and oil-based paints. Avoid cheap brushes that shed bristles, as they will ruin your finish. Next, you need rollers. A standard roller frame with a 230mm roller cover is ideal for walls. Use a short-nap roller for smooth surfaces and a long-nap roller for rough surfaces like stucco or brick. In many African markets, rollers are available in plastic or metal frames. Metal frames last longer. Also, get a roller tray and a roller screen to remove excess paint. For larger jobs, consider a paint sprayer. Airless sprayers are fast and give a smooth finish, but they are expensive. You can rent one for big projects. In Africa, rental services are available in major cities. If you cannot afford a sprayer, stick to brushes and rollers. You will also need a putty knife, a scraper, and a sanding block. These are used for surface preparation. A putty knife is for filling cracks and holes. A scraper removes old paint and loose material. A sanding block smooths surfaces. Get sandpaper in various grits: coarse for rough removal, medium for general smoothing, and fine for final finishing. For measuring and marking, carry a tape measure, a pencil, and a chalk line. A spirit level helps you draw straight lines. A ladder or scaffolding is essential for reaching high areas. In Africa, many painters use wooden ladders made locally. Ensure your ladder is sturdy and has non-slip feet. Now, let us discuss materials. Paint is your primary material. There are two main types: water-based (latex or acrylic) and oil-based (alkyd). Water-based paints are easy to clean up, dry quickly, and have low odour. They are ideal for interior walls and ceilings. Oil-based paints are durable, moisture-resistant, and give a hard finish. They are good for exterior wood and metal. In Africa, you will find many local paint brands such as Coral, Dulux, and Crown. There are also cheaper alternatives, but be careful: low-quality paint may fade quickly or peel. Always buy from reputable suppliers. You will also need primers. A primer seals the surface and helps paint adhere. For new cement walls, use an alkali-resistant primer. For wood, use a wood primer. For metal, use a rust-inhibiting primer. In coastal areas, choose a primer with anti-corrosive properties. Putty is used to fill cracks and holes. In Africa, you can buy ready-mixed putty or make your own using whiting and linseed oil. Ready-mixed is more convenient. You will also need sandpaper, masking tape, and drop cloths. Masking tape protects areas you do not want to paint, such as window frames and door handles. Drop cloths protect floors and furniture. In Africa, old newspapers or plastic sheets can serve as drop cloths. Do not skip these; they save you time on cleanup. Thinners and solvents are needed for cleaning oil-based paints. Use turpentine or mineral spirits. For water-based paints, just use soap and water. Always dispose of solvents properly. Do not pour them down drains or on the ground. They are toxic. Now, let us talk about sourcing. In Africa, you can find painting supplies at local hardware stores, building material markets, and even some supermarkets. In cities like Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, and Johannesburg, there are specialised paint shops. In rural areas, you may need to travel to a nearby town. Consider buying in bulk to save money. Many suppliers offer discounts for large orders. You can also join a buying group with other painters to negotiate better prices. Maintenance is key. Clean your brushes and rollers after every use. For water-based paint, wash with warm soapy water. For oil-based paint, use the appropriate solvent. Dry brushes with bristles facing down. Store them in a clean, dry place. Inspect your tools regularly. Replace worn-out brushes and rollers. A good brush can last for years if properly cared for. Finally, consider investing in a tool bag or box. This keeps your tools organised and easy to transport. In Africa, a sturdy plastic crate or a wooden box works well. Label your tools to avoid mix-ups on job sites. With the right tools and materials, you can deliver professional results. Remember, quality tools do not have to be expensive. Look for durable, functional items that suit your budget and your local market.

lessons.title: Surface Preparation: The Key to a Lasting Finish
lessons.body: Surface preparation is the most important step in any painting project. If you skip or rush this step, your paint will peel, blister, or flake. In Africa, surfaces vary widely: cement, mud, wood, metal, and stone. Each requires specific preparation. This lesson will guide you through the process for each type. First, let us cover general principles. Always start by cleaning the surface. Remove dust, dirt, grease, and loose paint. In dusty African environments, this is critical. Use a stiff brush or a broom to remove loose particles. For grease, use a degreaser or a mixture of soap and water. Rinse and let dry. Next, repair any damage. Fill cracks and holes with putty or a patching compound. For large holes, use a cement-based filler. Let it dry, then sand smooth. Sanding creates a rough surface that helps paint adhere. Use medium-grit sandpaper, then fine-grit for a smooth finish. Always sand in the direction of the grain for wood. For metal, sand to remove rust. Then apply a rust-inhibiting primer. Now, let us look at specific surfaces. Cement and plaster walls are common in Africa. New cement walls are highly alkaline. They can cause paint to saponify, meaning it turns into a soapy substance and peels. To prevent this, you must neutralise the alkalinity. Wash the wall with a solution of vinegar and water (1 part vinegar to 10 parts water). Or use a commercial alkali-resistant primer. Let the wall cure for at least 28 days before painting. This is important for new construction. For old cement walls, remove all loose paint and efflorescence (white salt deposits). Efflorescence indicates moisture. Find and fix the source of moisture before painting. Then apply a primer. Mud walls are common in rural Africa. They are porous and fragile. First, brush off loose mud. Then apply a stabiliser or a mud primer. This seals the surface and prevents the paint from soaking in too much. You may need two coats of primer. Use a breathable paint, such as lime wash or a silicate paint, to allow moisture to escape. Do not use oil-based paint on mud walls; it traps moisture and causes cracking. Wood surfaces are used for doors, windows, and furniture. Wood expands and contracts with humidity. In Africa, termites and borers are a threat. Treat wood with an insecticide and a fungicide before painting. Fill cracks with wood filler. Sand smooth. Apply a wood primer, then paint. For exterior wood, use a primer that resists moisture and UV. Metal surfaces include gates, railings, and roofs. Rust is the enemy. Remove rust with a wire brush or sandpaper. For heavy rust, use a chemical rust remover. Then apply a rust-inhibiting primer. For galvanised metal, use a special primer that etches the surface. In coastal areas, use a primer with zinc phosphate for extra protection. Stone surfaces are porous and uneven. Clean with a stiff brush and water. Use a masonry primer. For a natural look, you can leave some stone unpainted, but if you paint, use a breathable paint. Now, let us talk about tools for surface preparation. You will need a scraper, a wire brush, sandpaper, a sanding block, a putty knife, and a filling knife. For large areas, a power sander is helpful. In Africa, you can rent one. Also, use a damp cloth to wipe away dust after sanding. Do not use a dry cloth; it just spreads dust. Safety is crucial. Wear a dust mask when sanding, especially if the old paint contains lead. Lead paint is common in older buildings. If you suspect lead, use a lead test kit. If lead is present, follow safety guidelines: wear a respirator, cover the floor with plastic, and dispose of waste properly. In Africa, lead paint is still sold in some markets. Always check labels. Choose lead-free paints. Another important point is moisture. In many African regions, humidity is high. Do not paint if the surface is damp. Moisture trapped under paint causes blistering. Test for moisture by taping a piece of plastic to the surface. If condensation appears after a few hours, wait. Also, avoid painting in direct sunlight or extreme heat. The paint dries too fast, leading to brush marks and poor adhesion. Early morning or late afternoon is best. Finally, always prime. Primer is not optional. It seals, bonds, and protects. It also reduces the number of topcoats needed. A good primer can save you money on paint. In Africa, you can find affordable primers from local brands. Do not skip this step. In summary, surface preparation is hard work, but it is the foundation of a professional finish. Take your time, use the right products, and adapt to local conditions. Your clients will notice the difference, and your reputation will grow.

lessons.title: Painting Techniques for Professional Results
lessons.body: Now that you have prepared your surface, it is time to paint. This lesson covers the techniques that will give you a professional finish. We will discuss brushwork, roller application, spray painting, and special decorative effects. We will also cover common problems and how to fix them. Let us start with brushwork. Brushes are used for cutting in, which means painting edges and corners where a roller cannot reach. Hold the brush like a pencil, with your fingers near the bristles. Dip the brush about one-third into the paint. Tap off excess on the side of the can. Do not wipe it on the rim; that wastes paint. Apply the paint in a smooth, even stroke. Start a few centimetres away from the edge and brush towards it. This prevents paint from building up. For a straight line, use a steady hand. You can also use masking tape for crisp edges. In Africa, many painters use a technique called cutting in freehand. It takes practice. Keep a damp cloth handy to wipe mistakes. Next, rollers. Rollers cover large areas quickly. Choose the right nap for your surface. For smooth walls, use a short nap. For rough walls, use a long nap. Pour paint into a roller tray. Dip the roller and roll it back and forth on the tray screen to distribute paint evenly. Do not overload the roller. Start rolling in a large W pattern, then fill in without lifting the roller. Apply light pressure. For the best finish, roll in one direction for the final pass. If you are painting a ceiling, use a roller with an extension pole. Work in sections. Do not let the edges dry before you roll over them. This causes lap marks. Spray painting is fast and gives a smooth, even coat. It is ideal for large jobs, fences, and intricate metalwork. There are two types: airless and HVLP (high volume low pressure). Airless sprayers are powerful and can handle thick paints. HVLP sprayers are more precise and produce less overspray. In Africa, you can rent sprayers from equipment hire shops. Before spraying, mask off areas you do not want painted. Use drop cloths. Wear a respirator. Keep the sprayer moving at a consistent speed. Overlap each pass by 50 percent. Do not spray too close, or you will get runs. Do not spray too far, or you will get a dry, sandy finish. Practice on a piece of cardboard first. Now, let us talk about special decorative techniques. These can set you apart from other painters. One popular technique is sponging. Use a sea sponge to dab paint onto a base coat. This creates a textured, mottled look. Another is ragging. Use a crumpled cloth to roll or dab paint. This gives a soft, cloudy effect. Stencilling is also popular. Cut a design into a plastic sheet, place it on the wall, and apply paint with a stencil brush. In Africa, stencilling is used for borders and motifs. You can also do colour washing, which involves applying a thin glaze over a base coat and wiping it with a cloth. This creates a subtle, aged look. For a rustic finish, try dry brushing. Dip a brush in paint, wipe most of it off on a rag, then lightly drag the brush across the surface. This highlights texture. Another technique is faux finishing, such as marble or wood grain. These require practice and special tools. You can learn them through online tutorials or workshops. Now, let us cover common problems. One common issue is paint runs or drips. This happens when you apply too much paint. To fix, wait for the paint to dry, then sand smooth and repaint. Another issue is brush marks. This happens when you use a cheap brush or paint that is too thick. Use a good brush and thin the paint according to the manufacturer's instructions. Blistering is when paint bubbles up. This is usually caused by moisture under the paint. Find and fix the moisture source, then scrape, prime, and repaint. Peeling is when paint flakes off. This is due to poor surface preparation or incompatible paints. Remove loose paint, sand, prime, and repaint. Mildew is a problem in humid African regions. It appears as black or grey spots. Clean with a bleach solution, then use a mildew-resistant paint. Always test a small area first. Colour selection is also important. In Africa, colours can have cultural significance. For example, in many West African cultures, bright colours like yellow and red are used for celebrations. In East Africa, earth tones are popular. Consider the client's preferences and the building's style. Also, remember that colours look different under different lighting. Test a sample on the wall and view it at different times of day. Finally, always clean up after a job. Remove masking tape while the paint is still slightly wet. This prevents tearing. Clean your tools immediately. Dispose of paint cans and solvents properly. Do not leave a mess. A clean job site shows professionalism. With these techniques, you can deliver high-quality work that satisfies clients and builds your reputation. Practice regularly, and do not be afraid to experiment with new finishes.

lessons.title: Starting and Growing Your Painting Business in Africa
lessons.body: This final lesson of Module 1 focuses on the business side of painting and decorating. You have the skills; now you need to turn them into a profitable enterprise. We will cover legal registration, pricing, marketing, customer service, and financial management. Let us begin with legal registration. In many African countries, you can register a small business easily. In Kenya, for example, you can register a sole proprietorship through the eCitizen portal. In Nigeria, you can register with the Corporate Affairs Commission. In South Africa, you can register with the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission. Registration gives you a legal identity, allows you to open a business bank account, and makes you eligible for contracts. It also helps you build trust with clients. If registration is too expensive or complex, start as a sole proprietor and upgrade later. Next, pricing. Pricing is one of the hardest parts of running a painting business. You must cover your costs and make a profit. First, calculate your costs: paint, primers, putty, sandpaper, masking tape, drop cloths, tools, transport, and labour. Add a markup for profit, usually 20 to 30 percent. Then, estimate the time the job will take. For example, if a room takes two days and you want to earn 10,000 naira per day, your labour cost is 20,000 naira. Add material costs. That is your price. Do not undercharge. Many African painters make this mistake. They compete on price and end up working for nothing. Instead, compete on quality and reliability. Offer a written quote. Include a breakdown of costs. This transparency builds trust. You can also offer different packages: basic, standard, and premium. For example, basic might be one coat of paint, standard two coats, premium includes surface repair and a decorative finish. Now, marketing. How will clients find you? Start with your network. Tell friends, family, and neighbours. Word of mouth is powerful in Africa. Ask satisfied clients for referrals. Create a simple portfolio. Take before and after photos. Print them or save them on your phone. Use social media. WhatsApp is widely used. Create a business profile. Post photos of your work. Join local community groups on Facebook. Offer a special discount for the first five clients who book through social media. You can also print flyers and posters. Place them in hardware stores, community centres, and churches. Partner with real estate agents. They often need painters for rental properties. Visit construction sites and talk to contractors. Leave your business card. Consider a sign on your vehicle or a branded t-shirt. Consistency is key. Post regularly. Respond to messages quickly. Customer service is critical. Arrive on time. Be polite. Listen to the client's needs. If you make a mistake, fix it immediately. Do not argue. A happy client will recommend you. A dissatisfied client will tell everyone. Always provide a written contract. It should include the scope of work, start and end dates, payment schedule, and warranty. A simple one-page contract is fine. Ask for a deposit, usually 50 percent, to buy materials. The balance is paid on completion. For large jobs, arrange progress payments. Now, financial management. Keep business and personal money separate. Open a bank account or use a mobile money account. In Africa, mobile money like M-Pesa, Airtel Money, and MTN Mobile Money is convenient. Track your income and expenses. Use a notebook or a simple spreadsheet. Save for taxes. In many countries, small businesses pay a presumptive tax. Check with your local tax authority. Also, save for equipment upgrades and emergencies. Reinvest in your business. Buy better tools, a vehicle, or training for yourself. Consider hiring helpers. When you have more work than you can handle, hire one or two assistants. Pay them fairly. Train them in your methods. This allows you to take on bigger projects. But do not expand too fast. Make sure you have consistent work before hiring. Finally, think about growth. You can expand into related services: wallpaper installation, decorative finishes, waterproofing, and even interior design. You can also target commercial clients: offices, hotels, schools, and hospitals. These jobs are larger and more lucrative. To win them, you need a professional presentation. Create a company profile. Include your registration certificate, tax compliance, and references. Bid on tenders. Many African governments and NGOs publish tenders for painting contracts. Check their websites. In conclusion, painting and decorating is a viable business in Africa. With skill, professionalism, and smart business practices, you can build a successful career. Remember to always deliver quality work, treat clients with respect, and manage your money wisely. This module has given you the foundation. Now it is time to take action. Start small, learn from every job, and never stop improving. Your future as a professional painter and decorator in Africa is bright.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pricing, Estimating and Health-Safe Practices for African Painters

In African markets, painting and decorating is a business before it is a craft. A painter who can quote accurately, protect workers from chemical exposure, and choose the right product for a dusty, humid, or high-sun environment will win repeat contracts. This practical reference lesson consolidates the numbers, formulas, and safety rules that determine whether a job makes a profit or a loss. It is written for the working painter, the small contractor, and the apprentice who wants to move from day-labour to running a registered enterprise.

Across the continent, demand is rising: rapid urbanisation, a growing middle class, hospitality and retail expansion, and government housing programmes all drive paint consumption. But competition is fierce, and the biggest killers of small painting businesses are underpricing, over-ordering materials, and ignoring occupational health. This lesson gives you the tools to avoid all three.

1. Estimating Paint Quantity Accurately

Under-ordering causes delays and return trips; over-ordering ties up cash that a small business cannot spare. The standard industry rule is that one litre of quality emulsion covers approximately 10â12 mÂ² per coat on a smooth, properly prepared surface. On rough or porous substrates common in African construction â sand-cement render, roughcast, or previously unpainted blockwork â coverage can drop to 6â8 mÂ² per litre. Always measure, never guess.

The formula for a rectangular wall is straightforward: Area = Height Ã Width. For a full room, sum the four walls, subtract doors and windows, then multiply by the number of coats (usually two for emulsion, one primer plus two topcoats for new work). Add a 10% waste allowance for African site conditions: wind, high temperatures, roller loss, and touch-ups.

Table 1: Paint coverage and quantity estimates by substrate type (per 10 mÂ², two coats)
Substrate Coverage per litre (mÂ²) Litres needed for 10 mÂ², 2 coats Primer required
Smooth plaster / skim coat 12 1.7 L 1 coat, 0.8 L
Sand-cement render 9 2.2 L 1 coat, 1.1 L
Roughcast / textured 7 2.9 L 1 coat, 1.4 L
Bare blockwork 6 3.3 L 2 coats, 2.0 L
Previously painted, sound 11 1.8 L Spot prime only

Source: Coverage figures adapted from manufacturer technical data sheets (Dulux, Crown Paints Kenya, Plascon) and ILO construction training materials. Actual coverage varies with application method, temperature, and dilution.

2. Labour-Day Estimating and Pricing

Labour is the largest cost line in most African painting contracts. A common mistake is to quote a lump sum without calculating labour days. Use this method:

  1. Measure total paintable area (mÂ²).
  2. Apply a productivity rate: a competent painter with a roller covers 25â35 mÂ² per day for emulsion on smooth walls; 15â20 mÂ² per day for textured or detailed work; 8â12 mÂ² per day for gloss on trim and doors.
  3. Divide total area by productivity rate to get labour days.
  4. Multiply by the local daily rate, then add 30â40% for supervision, statutory contributions, and downtime.

For example, a 300 mÂ² interior repaint at 30 mÂ²/day = 10 painter-days. At a Nairobi or Lagos daily rate of USD 15â25, that is USD 150â250 in direct labour. Add 35% overhead = USD 203â338. Then add paint, materials, and profit margin. If you quoted USD 400 for the whole job, you would be working for almost nothing.

Table 2: Indicative daily labour rates and productivity for painters in selected African markets (2023â2024)
Country / city Daily rate (USD, unskilled) Daily rate (USD, skilled) Productivity (mÂ²/day, emulsion)
Kenya (Nairobi) 8â12 15â25 25â35
Nigeria (Lagos) 7â11 14â22 20â30
Ghana (Accra) 6â10 12â20 22â32
South Africa (Johannesburg) 18â25 30â45 28â38
Tanzania (Dar es Salaam) 5â9 10â18 20â28

Source: Rates compiled from ILO (2023) Global Wage Report, national construction authority wage schedules, and field interviews with contractors. Figures are indicative and exclude statutory benefits, transport, and tools.

â  CHEMICAL SAFETY WARNING

Solvent-based paints, thinners, and two-pack epoxy or polyurethane coatings contain volatile organic compounds (VOCs), isocyanates, and heavy metals (lead, chromium, cadmium). Exposure causes respiratory disease, dermatitis, neurological damage, and â with lead-based paints â irreversible harm to children. In many African markets, lead paint is still sold and used despite bans.

Mandatory controls: Always work in ventilated spaces; wear a fitted respirator (not a dust mask) when spraying two-pack systems; use nitrile gloves, not latex; wear eye protection; never eat, drink, or smoke on site; wash hands and forearms before breaks; store solvents away from living areas and out of reach of children.

If you experience dizziness, headache, or breathing difficulty, stop work immediately, move to fresh air, and seek medical attention. Report any suspected lead paint to your national environmental or health authority.

3. Protecting the Business and the Worker

Health and safety is not a cost â it is a business asset. A painter who is sick cannot work, and a contractor with an injured worker faces liability, lost contracts, and reputational damage. International buyers, NGOs, and government tenders in Africa increasingly require evidence of occupational health compliance. Simple measures â gloves, respirators, hand-washing stations, and a written safety briefing â cost less than 2% of a typical contract value but reduce accident risk dramatically.

From a commercial angle, safety compliance lets you bid for higher-value work: hospital repaints, school refurbishments, food-processing facilities, and donor-funded housing. These clients ask for method statements, material safety data sheets (MSDS), and proof of training. Preparing these documents once gives you a reusable tender pack that opens doors your competitors cannot enter.

4. Environmental and Climate Considerations in Africa

African painting conditions are harsh. High UV radiation fades cheap pigments within months. Harmattan dust and coastal humidity cause adhesion failures. Termites and mould attack organic-based fillers. Specify exterior paints with UV-stable pigments and fungicide additives. Avoid painting in direct sun above 35Â°C or on damp surfaces â adhesion and curing suffer. In coastal West Africa, choose anti-corrosive primers on metal; inland, choose breathable masonry paints to manage moisture.

Water-based (acrylic emulsion) paints are preferred over solvent-based for interiors: lower VOC, easier clean-up, faster drying, and lower cost. Reserve solvent-based products for metal, high-wear surfaces, and where a specific technical requirement exists. This choice reduces health risk, lowers insurance premiums, and aligns with green building trends that are growing in African cities.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Measure twice, quote once: Calculate wall area, subtract openings, multiply by coats, add 10% waste.
  • Never guess labour: Divide area by productivity rate (25â35 mÂ²/day emulsion) to get painter-days.
  • Add 30â40% overhead for supervision, transport, tools, and statutory costs before adding profit.
  • Check the substrate: Bare block needs two primer coats; roughcast uses 40% more paint.
  • Wear a respirator, nitrile gloves, and eye protection when using solvent or two-pack products.
  • Keep an MSDS file for every product on site â required for tenders and emergencies.
  • Store paint and solvents away from food, children, and living areas; never decant into drink bottles.
  • Reinvest 10% of each contract in tools, training, and a safety kit â this is how you grow from painter to contractor.

Further Reading

  • ILO â Occupational Safety and Health in Construction (free training materials and codes of practice).
  • WHO â Lead Poisoning and Health Fact Sheet (essential for lead-paint awareness and prevention).
  • FAO â Rural Infrastructure and Construction Guidelines (relevant for rural painting and finishing projects).
  • UNEP â Global Alliance to Eliminate Lead Paint (regulatory and market guidance for African countries).
  • ILO â Start Your Business: Small Enterprise Development (free business planning and costing workbook).

Mastering these practical reference tools â accurate estimating, safe chemical handling, and smart product selection â turns painting from a hand-to-mouth trade into a scalable African enterprise. The painters who win the next decade will be those who quote with numbers, protect their crews, and document their work for the clients who pay best.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a primer when painting a surface?
options: A) To add decorative texture
B) To seal the surface and improve paint adhesion
C) To provide the final colour finish
D) To clean the surface before painting
quiz.explanation: Primer seals porous surfaces and creates a bond that helps the topcoat adhere properly and last longer.

quiz.q: Which tool is best suited for cutting in along ceilings and skirting boards?
options: A) Roller
B) Paint sprayer
C) Angled sash brush
D) Sponge
quiz.explanation: An angled sash brush gives precise control for cutting in neat edges along ceilings and skirting boards.

quiz.q: What does the term cutting in refer to in painting and decorating?
options: A) Mixing two paint colours together
B) Removing old wallpaper
C) Trimming wallpaper edges
D) Painting edges and corners with a brush before rolling
quiz.explanation: Cutting in means brushing paint along edges, corners and trim so the roller can fill the main area without touching adjacent surfaces.

quiz.q: Which type of paint is most commonly used for interior walls and ceilings?
options: A) Emulsion
B) Gloss
C) Varnish
D) Wood stain
quiz.explanation: Emulsion is a water based paint designed for interior walls and ceilings because it is easy to apply and clean up.

quiz.q: Why is it important to sand a surface between coats of paint?
options: A) To change the colour of the paint
B) To remove dust and create a smooth key for the next coat
C) To make the paint dry faster
D) To increase the paint volume
quiz.explanation: Sanding removes imperfections and dust and provides a key so the next coat bonds smoothly.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for preparing a previously painted interior wall?
options: A) Apply topcoat then clean then sand
B) Clean, sand, fill defects, then prime bare spots
C) Fill defects then apply topcoat then clean
D) Sand then apply topcoat then fill defects
quiz.explanation: Proper preparation involves cleaning, sanding, filling any defects and priming bare areas before painting.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a health and safety requirement when painting indoors?
options: A) Keep all windows closed at all times
B) Store paint near a heat source
C) Ensure adequate ventilation and wear appropriate PPE
D) Eat and drink in the work area
quiz.explanation: Good ventilation and suitable personal protective equipment reduce exposure to fumes and hazardous substances.

quiz.q: What is the main reason for applying a mist coat to new plaster?
options: A) To make the plaster waterproof
B) To add a glossy finish
C) To hide imperfections in the plaster
D) To seal the porous surface and prevent the topcoat from being absorbed unevenly
quiz.explanation: A mist coat is a diluted emulsion that soaks into new plaster to seal it so the topcoat adheres and dries evenly.
